mechanism_name: TXCZ OEM watchdog/OTA service restoring /system from a golden image (txcz_ota)
how_it_works: Hypothesis: txcz_ota (or a native helper daemon it installs/execs, alongside sibling txcz_app/txcz_launcher/txczbox/txcztest packages under com.shzhtxcz.txbox) is a vendor-added integrity/anti-tamper component that keeps a 'golden' reference copy of some /system content -- potentially as small as /system/etc/init/hw/init.rc, or as large as a full system.img/tar -- stored somewhere not exposed as a named by-name partition: bundled as a raw or compressed asset inside another txcz_* APK (res/raw or assets/), tucked into a hidden dotdir under /data (e.g. /data/txcz*, /data/.txcz, /data/misc/txcz), or written into unallocated/reserved eMMC space ahead of the first GPT-declared partition. On each real boot, the theory goes, this component computes a hash or diff of the live files against the reference and, on mismatch, copies the golden content back over the live ext4 files (or the whole /system logical partition) before or shortly after the affected subsystem would otherwise take effect, optionally forcing a second silent reboot to make the restored init.rc take effect cleanly. If implemented as an ordinary Android app/service, its natural trigger point is a BOOT_COMPLETED broadcast receiver or an early 'persist.sys.*'-gated service started from init.rc itself (i.e. still inside the second-stage init/Zygote/system_server timeline), since a plain APK component cannot execute before the OS that hosts the Dalvik/ART runtime has itself been brought up by init.
fits_observed_symptoms: (1) Write succeeds and is confirmed present pre-reboot: trivially fits -- irrelevant to this mechanism, it only describes the starting state. (2) Survives unmount/remount within the same recovery session: fits -- a boot-triggered watchdog/OTA app or service simply never runs during a live recovery mount (no Android boot, no Zygote, no BOOT_COMPLETED), so nothing invokes it. (3) Reverts only after a real power-cycle boot: fits loosely -- consistent with any mechanism gated on an actual boot, but does not by itself distinguish an app-level restorer from an earlier bootloader/first-stage-init restorer. (4) The boot_completed marker-file write added to init.rc never appears in /cache: this is the mechanism's weakest point and explains the symptom POORLY as literally described. A BOOT_COMPLETED-triggered Java/native app cannot begin executing until second-stage init has already fully parsed init.rc, started Zygote, and system_server has set sys.boot_completed=1 -- by which point init's own in-process 'on boot_completed' trigger (which needs only a fork+exec, no app cold-start) should fire at essentially the same time as or before any app-level receiver, so the marker file should have been written on that boot even if txcz_ota then reverted init.rc for the NEXT boot. Its total absence instead implies init.rc was already reverted before second-stage init ever parsed it -- earlier than any userspace APK component can act. A same-boot 'app restores then wipes /cache and silently reboots' chain could technically explain the absence, but is a more contrived, unverified assumption than a pre-init-parse actor. (5) AVB/vbmeta already fully disabled: fits well -- this mechanism doesn't depend on AVB at all, so it works identically whether or not verified boot is enforcing, and it's a plausible reason an OEM would add its own tamper-response layer independent of (and possibly instead of) Google's AVB. (6) /system is ext4, not squashfs: neutral/consistent -- a writable ext4 filesystem is exactly what makes a live file-level 'reapply golden copy' step both possible and necessary (an immutable squashfs image wouldn't need active reversion in the first place). (7) Device is non-A/B: fits contextually -- ruled out as the explanation is a same-boot A/B-slot swap, leaving room for an active restorer of some kind, of which an OEM watchdog is one candidate; it does not by itself favor an app-level implementation over other candidate actors evaluated separately (e.g. a compiled-in first-stage restore or reserved-eMMC golden image).
known_precedent: No public documentation of com.shzhtxcz.txbox, txcz_ota, or any 'TXCZ' branded self-healing/anti-tamper mechanism was found; TXCZ (Shenzhen Tianxing Chuangzhan Electronics, board marking TXCZ_HD3128/TXCZ-SDK) appears in only a handful of XDA teardown/rooting threads and device-fingerprint aggregator sites, confirming it is an undocumented, generic Rockchip STB/projector reference-design vendor rather than one with published engineering documentation -- so this specific claim is unverifiable from public sources and should be treated as speculative [uncertain]. The closest real, well-documented AOSP-standard precedent for the general PATTERN (an OEM/AOSP-shipped component that reflashes partition content from an embedded reference copy at boot to defeat persistent tampering) is the stock install-recovery.sh / flash_recovery service: init.rc runs /system/bin/install-recovery.sh via a 'flash_recovery' service at boot, which compares a stored checksum against the recovery partition and reapplies an embedded binary patch (recovery-from-boot.p) if it detects drift -- this establishes that boot-time, checksum-gated, embedded-reference-copy restoration is a real and long-standing (since Android ICS/Gingerbread) part of the Android ecosystem, even though its canonical AOSP use targets the recovery partition, not /system or init.rc. Separately, community threads about rooting cheap Rockchip-based TV boxes (RK3566/RK3568, RK3229, RK3128) repeatedly describe file-level reversion / DM-verity-and-FEC-like persistence problems on this device class, but these are anecdotal forum reports, not primary vendor documentation, and do not confirm an app-driven mechanism specifically.
likelihood: Low-medium. The pattern (OEM boot-time self-healing from an embedded reference copy) is real and precedented in AOSP (install-recovery.sh), but the specific claim that a userspace app like txcz_ota performs the restore is undercut by the marker-file timing evidence, which points to a revert that happens before second-stage init even parses init.rc -- earlier than any Android app can run; decompiling txcz_ota is still worthwhile to confirm or rule this out cheaply before chasing lower-level candidates.
test_procedure: All commands run from the existing adb-root Recovery shell against the manually mounted, writable ext4 /system; nothing here reboots the device except step 6, which is optional and explicitly a controlled reboot cycle. 1) Locate and pull the OEM apps for offline decompilation: `pm list packages | grep -i txcz` (if pm works in this context) or directly `find /system -iname '*txcz*'` to enumerate txcz_ota/txcz_app/txcz_launcher/txczbox/txcztest APK/ODEX paths, then `adb pull /system/priv-app/<TxczOta>/ .` (or wherever found) to a workstation for jadx/apktool decompilation (out of scope for the recovery shell itself, but the pull is the actionable step here). 2) Cheap in-shell triage without a host decompiler: `unzip -o <path-to-txcz_ota.apk> -d /data/local/tmp/txcz_x` then grep the extracted AndroidManifest.xml and classes.dex for boot-time hooks and restore-flavored strings: `strings /data/local/tmp/txcz_x/AndroidManifest.xml | grep -i BOOT_COMPLETED` and `strings /data/local/tmp/txcz_x/classes*.dex | grep -iE 'golden|backup|restore|checksum|md5|sha1|watchdog|selfheal|init\.rc|/system/etc'`. 3) Check for an embedded reference image inside the APK's own assets/res: `unzip -l <path-to-txcz_ota.apk> | grep -iE '\.img$|\.tar|\.gz|assets/|raw/'` and, for any hit, `unzip -p <apk> <entry> | strings | grep -F 'on boot_completed'` (or another line unique to your ORIGINAL, pre-edit init.rc) to check for a literal embedded copy. 4) Search /data and /system for a hidden reference directory: `find /data -maxdepth 4 \( -iname '*txcz*' -o -iname '.*' \) -type d 2>/dev/null` and `find / -xdev -iname '*golden*' -o -iname '*.system.bak*' 2>/dev/null`. 5) Distinguish 'byte-range edit scrubbed' from 'whole-file restored from image': before your next edit, note `stat /system/etc/init/hw/init.rc` (mtime/inode), make the edit, reboot, re-enter recovery, and `stat` again -- an mtime/inode that reverts to the ORIGINAL pre-edit value indicates a whole-file replace (consistent with a stored golden copy being written back), while a NEW mtime with the edit gone would indicate live in-place scrubbing by a running process instead (a different mechanism entirely). 6) Correlate with boot-time logs: after a normal (non-recovery) boot, pull `/proc/last_kmsg` or `/sys/fs/pstore/console-ramoops*` if present, and check `logcat -b all -d | grep -iE 'txcz|ota|integrity|verify'` for any OEM service tag that logs a restore action -- if the revert truly predates init.rc parsing, expect NO txcz_ota logcat activity correlated with it, which would itself be evidence against this mechanism and should be weighed alongside steps 1-5.
bypass_or_fix: If steps 1-4 confirm a concrete restore path (a BOOT_COMPLETED receiver plus an embedded/hidden reference copy, or an init.rc service stanza that execs a native txcz watchdog binary): (a) Disable the offending app so PackageManager can't load or run it: rename the APK directory so it's invisible to scanning, e.g. `mv /system/priv-app/txcz_ota /system/priv-app/txcz_ota.disabled` (do this for any sibling txcz_* package found to host the same behavior), and if pm is functional, also `pm disable-user --user 0 <package.name>` as a belt-and-suspenders step. (b) If a native binary is exec'd directly from an init.rc `service` stanza (not from an app), comment out or delete that service block in init.rc so it never starts. (c) Neutralize the reference copy itself so even a resurrected instance has nothing to restore from -- delete the hidden /data directory or embedded asset identified in test steps 3-4 (back it up off-device first). (d) Re-run the mtime/diff check from test step 5 across a fresh reboot cycle to confirm init.rc now persists. Keep a full backup of /system and any deleted files before making these changes, since disabling an OEM component blindly risks side effects unrelated to this specific hypothesis (e.g. breaking a legitimate update mechanism or triggering an unrelated factory-reset failsafe).
risk_level: Steps 1-4 and 6 are read-only diagnostics (pull, unzip -l/-p, strings, find, stat, logcat) and carry no risk to the device. Step 5 requires one real reboot cycle per test iteration; low risk since the device is already known to boot successfully through this revert behavior repeatedly, but each cycle costs time and should be minimized. bypass_or_fix actions (renaming/disabling an OEM system app, editing init.rc service stanzas, deleting a suspected reference file) are MEDIUM risk: they are reversible in principle (restore the renamed/backed-up files) but could disable a component load-bearing for something other than this hypothesis, or trigger an OEM tamper-response (e.g. a factory-reset failsafe) if the assumption about what the app does is wrong -- always keep an off-device backup of /system and any files removed before applying the fix.
